venue_now: No archival venue: the page header reads 'Preprint. Under review.' and the text is arXiv:2504.06260v1, 8 Apr 2025 (p. 1), the latest version. papers.json records NeurIPS 2024 workshops (MATH-AI; Open-World Agents) from the arXiv comment alone
what_it_is: A benchmark of whether LLMs and LLM agents can solve physics, mathematics and engineering problems end to end with finite element analysis, by reading a natural-language problem and generating Java API calls that build and solve a model in COMSOL Multiphysics (pp. 1-3). FEABench Gold has 15 problems derived from COMSOL Application Gallery tutorials, each manually verified to be self-sufficient and solvable, with a target value, a step-by-step plan, ground-truth code and a model tree; FEABench Large has 200 algorithmically parsed tutorials without a single verifiable target (pp. 2-3, 7). Evaluation combines execution and solution-path metrics (executability, model-tree similarity to the ground truth, physics-interface and feature recall, feature dimension) with an LLM-checked target value and its relative error (pp. 5-6, 19-23). Six LLMs are tested at baseline, and a multi-turn agent with tools and execution feedback is built on Gemini-1.5-Pro (pp. 4-9).
domain: engineering and physics simulation with finite element analysis (heat transfer, structural and eigenfrequency problems, a quantum dot, even a Black-Scholes option model) (pp. 1, 3)
size: 15 Gold problems, each in two task versions (ModelSpecs and Plan), and 200 Large tasks; a 768-snippet annotated code library is used only for retrieval, not evaluation (pp. 2-3). 6 LLMs at baseline (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-Pro, Gemma-2-27B-IT, Gemma-2-9B-IT, CodeGemma-7B-IT) plus prompting and agent variants on Gemini-1.5-Pro (pp. 6-9)
source_of_items: derived from public COMSOL Multiphysics Application Gallery tutorials; for Gold, the first 2-3 specifications were written by an expert COMSOL user and the rest drafted by an LLM from the tutorials, then verified and edited by people (pp. 3, 15)
has_gold_traces: partial: each Gold problem has a step-by-step Plan (natural-language COMSOL instructions), ground-truth API code that computes the target, and a model tree (pp. 3, 15-19). These are software-action solution paths, not reasoning traces; the paper calls the model tree 'a high-level lossy representation of a solution path' (p. 3)
evaluation: execution and solution-path metrics plus the final value: executability (share of parsed API lines that run), Model Tree Score (similarity of the built model tree to the ground truth's), physics metrics (interface factuality; interface, feature and feature-property recall against the ground-truth code; feature dimension), Valid Target (Gemini-1.5-Pro judges whether the exported table holds the target quantity) and Relative Error | Strict (within 10%) (pp. 5-6, 19-23)
human_validation: Gold problems manually confirmed self-sufficient and solvable, and the ground-truth code manually verified to export the target value (pp. 2, 15). FEABench Large is not human-verified (pp. 3, 7). The LLM that judges Valid Target is not validated against people, and no inter-annotator figures are reported
contamination_measures: none; the problems derive from public COMSOL tutorials that are 'accessible on the internet' (pp. 3, 10)

engtrace_use.sentence: S-E2 (L190-198): 'Others focus on tangential skills such as design generation (Guo et al., 2025b) or software proficiency (Mudur et al., 2025), while broader efforts like EngiBench (Zhou et al., 2025) rely on subjective rubric-based scoring.' S-I3c (L116-122): 'EngTrace addresses both gaps through integrative reasoning templates that, unlike existing benchmarks (e.g., Zhou et al., 2025; Mudur et al., 2025) that rely solely on outcome matching, demand holistic procedural reasoning'. S-E3 (L199-205, closing): 'Evidently, existing benchmarks remain limited to outcome matching and fail to validate the physically grounded reasoning required for engineering.'
engtrace_use.explanation: S-E2 (imprecise): operating COMSOL through its API is central, and the paper finds that translating decisions into valid calls is the larger bottleneck (p. 8), so 'software proficiency' is not baseless. But the benchmark is built and scored to measure physics reasoning as well: correct physics decisions such as boundary conditions and spatial dimensions (p. 2), physics metrics described as 'a granular look into the LLM's physics reasoning path' (p. 6), and feature dimension called 'a correctness and physics reasoning metric' (p. 23); the title says 'Multiphysics Reasoning Ability' (p. 1). S-I3c (misleading, the protocol's own example of calling a benchmark outcome-only when it also scores intermediate work): FEABench's stated contribution is 'a holistic automated evaluation strategy with intermediate metrics' measuring 'distance to a correct solution' (p. 2), and it argues that pass@k-style outcome metrics fail here because most solutions never compute the target (p. 5). In the COMSOL experiments a valid target is reached on at most 2 of the 15 Gold problems (pp. 7, 9), so the reported results rest mainly on the intermediate metrics (pp. 6-9). S-E3 is contradicted for this paper on the same grounds.

suggested_wording: FEABench (Mudur et al., 2025) has models solve multiphysics problems by generating COMSOL Multiphysics API calls, and scores the solution path (executability, similarity of the built model to the ground truth, recall of its physics features) as well as the computed target on 15 hand-verified problems; what it compares with a reference are software actions, not the steps of a derivation.
facts_to_cite: 15 manually verified Gold problems and 200 algorithmically parsed Large tasks, both from COMSOL Application Gallery tutorials (pp. 2-3).
Models must generate Java API calls that build the model in COMSOL Multiphysics and export a target value (pp. 2-3).

Metrics include executability, a model-tree similarity score against the ground truth, physics-interface, feature and property recall, feature dimension, an LLM-checked valid target and relative error within 10% (pp. 5-6, 19-23).
The best strategy, a multi-turn agent with tools and execution feedback, produces executable API calls 88% of the time (pp. 1, 9).
No COMSOL configuration computes a valid target on more than 2 of the 15 Gold problems (pp. 7, 9); a Python SWE-agent computes one on 11 but passes the strict 10% cut on only 4 (p. 9).
Translating modelling decisions into valid API calls is a larger bottleneck than making the decisions (p. 8).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: an engineering and physics domain with physical quantities; a reference solution path per problem (plan, ground-truth code, model tree; p. 3); evaluation of intermediate work against that reference, not only the final value (pp. 5-6); hand verification of problems (pp. 2, 15). Lacks: generated instances (15 static problems from public tutorials, pp. 3, 10); reasoning traces (its references are software actions, p. 3); verification of numerical reasoning steps (its intermediate metrics score code and model structure, pp. 19-23); expert validation of its evaluator (the Valid Target LLM judge is unvalidated, p. 21); contamination measures (none). It is a different task: tool use with a commercial solver rather than reasoning in text.
notes: The execution-based metrics need a COMSOL licence (p. 10). The single 'strict' pass was serendipitous: the exported value, about 20 degrees Celsius, is a COMSOL default, against a target of 18.3 (p. 9). In Appendix G a Python SWE-agent computes a valid target on 11 problems but passes the strict cut on 4 (p. 9). Zhou et al.'s EngiBench classifies FEABench as 'task-oriented' evaluation (zhou2025engibench p. 3), a better label than 'outcome matching'.
